newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HORN SAYS HUNGARY COALITION NOT HIT BY RESIGNATION.
newsitem.headline: HORN SAYS HUNGARY COALITION NOT HIT BY RESIGNATION.

text.p: Hungary's Prime Minister Gyula Horn said the resignation on Monday of the president of the junior governing coalition partner would not weaken the coalition.

"I was very sorry to hear of Mr Peto's decision," Horn told reporters. "I don't think this should affect or weaken coalition cooperation because there are a number of joint enterprises that extend to the end of the parliamentary year."

Horn, leader of the Socialist Party, heads a coalition of the Socialists and the the Alliance of Free Democrats (SZDSZ) which has 72 percent of parliamentary seats. The Socialists alone hold 54 percent.

A source close to the party who wished to remain anonymous told Reuters thatn Peto's resignation could be linked with a privatisation scandal involving $5 million of irregular payments to an independent consultant hired by the State Privatisation Agency APV to negotiate land deals in 1996.

A businessman close to the SZSDSZ is alleged to have received money from the adviser, Marta Tocsik, and Peto has been frequently criticised by his political opponents for not taking political responsibility in the affair.
The treasurer of the Socialist Party has also been implicated in the affair.
Peto offered to resign over the scandal late last year but was persuaded by his party to stay on.

Peto, who is not a minister in Horn's government, resigned as SZDSZ president and parliamentary leader on Monday but did not cite an official reason. He was expected to make a further statement later in the day.
Peto announced his decision at an extraordinary meeting of the party's national executive, which will call a national party congress next month, Hungarian news agency MTI reported.

SZDSZ Interior Minister Gabor Kuncze will act as caretaker party leader until a successor is appointed. The SZDSZ parliamentary group will be lead by Istvan Szent-Ivanyi, who is currently state secretary at the Foreign Ministry.
